title: Similarity
explain: Once items are vectors, similarity is a number saying how alike two vectors are. The workhorse is cosine similarity, the cosine of the angle between them: it compares direction and ignores length, so a document pasted three times still scores 1.0 against the original. (余弦相似度: 看方向, 不看长度.)
model:
`cos(a, b) = (a . b) / (|a| |b|)`

Range: `1` same direction, `0` orthogonal (unrelated), `-1` opposite. Non-negative vectors (TF-IDF) stay in `[0, 1]`.

Example: `(3,4)` and `(4,3)`: `a . b = 24`, `|a| = |b| = 5`, so cos = `24/25 = 0.96`.

| Measure | Looks at | Magnitude | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cosine | angle | ignored | text/semantic similarity |
| Dot product `a . b` | angle and length | kept | recommenders (popularity or confidence adds score) |
| Euclidean distance `d(a, b)` | straight-line gap | kept | clustering, [k-means](#/sd/f/k-means) |

**Normalize once.** If every vector has length 1, then `cos = dot` and `|a - b|^2 = 2 - 2 cos`. All three measures then rank neighbours identically, and the plain dot product is the cheapest to compute.

Used by [similarity search](#/sd/f/similarity-search) over [item embeddings](#/sd/f/item-embedding).

details.q: Why cosine instead of Euclidean distance for text?
details.a: Length usually carries no meaning for text: article B is article A pasted three times, so every count is tripled. The direction is identical (cosine 1.0) but the Euclidean distance is large. Cosine compares what the document is about, not how long it is.

details.q: When would you use the dot product instead?
details.a: When magnitude is a signal. Many recommenders train embeddings so that a longer vector means a more popular or more confident item, and ranking by dot product lets that boost the score. Use whichever the model was trained with.

details.q: What does a cosine of 0 mean?
details.a: Orthogonal, not opposite. For sparse non-negative vectors it simply means no overlapping weighted terms: no evidence of relatedness in this representation. Opposite directions (-1) only appear with signed dense embeddings.

details.q: What changes if all vectors are L2-normalized?
details.a: The denominator of cosine becomes 1, so cosine equals the dot product, and `|a - b|^2 = 2 - 2 cos`. Rankings by cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance coincide. Two unit vectors with cosine 0.8 have squared distance 0.4. Normalize at write time and use dot product at query time.

details.q: How do you compute a quick example by hand?
details.a: For `(1,2,2)` and `(2,1,2)`: dot product `2+2+4 = 8`, both lengths 3, cosine `8/9`, about 0.89. Always compute dot, then the two norms, then divide.

details.q: Is a high cosine score a probability or a threshold you can reuse?
details.a: No. The scale depends on the model, so 0.8 can be 'very close' in one embedding space and 'barely related' in another. Pick thresholds empirically per model and re-check them after any model change.

prompts.q: Explain cosine similarity and why it ignores length.
points: cos = dot product over the product of lengths
Euclidean distance would call it far

prompts.q: Compare cosine, dot product and Euclidean distance and say when each fits.
points: Cosine ignores magnitude, good for semantic text
On unit vectors all three rank the same
Match the metric the model was trained with

prompts.q: Why normalize embeddings once at write time?
points: Unit length makes cos equal to dot
Index libraries can use inner product directly
